checked_sources: Independent finite check: python3 /workspace/branches/frozen_math_reproduction.py dumbbell; directly enumerated pair partitions and neighborhood domination for 3600 subsets of 16 graphs with 2≤r,s≤5, and checked polynomial agreement at 11 distinct integers for every graph.
correctness.rationale: Since r,s≥2, each clique has a non-bridge vertex and must be hit by any dominating set. Hitting both cliques is sufficient. In a perfect matching the sole bridge is either absent, leaving two positive even selected clique sizes, or present, forcing both endpoints and odd selected sizes on both sides. Complete graphs on even selected cardinalities have perfect matchings, so these disjoint conditions are both sufficient. Counting selected sets rather than matchings gives the product of the positive even sums and the product of the even sums on non-bridge vertices times x². All degrees and edge cases follow, including r=s=2, where the polynomial is x²+x⁴. The sole size-two set is the bridge pair, and the two products at x=1 are the stated total.
residual_risks: The independent finite check covers only the stated range. The no-cross-or-one-cross pairing argument proves the infinite result.

evidence: The complete-multipartite formula in the record ending ea2bc935cbba is inapplicable: a non-bridge vertex of one clique is nonadjacent to both endpoints of an edge in the other clique, impossible in a complete multipartite graph. The fully whiskered theorem ending bb4750808ce7 includes W(K2)=P4; larger clique dumbbells are not fully whiskered (they have fewer than half their vertices of degree one).
broader_coverage.reasoning: The strongest available broader-class formulas settle only the stated boundary or do not apply. No coefficientwise bridge recurrence covering arbitrary r and s was found in the bounded lookups, not a claim of its nonexistence.

value.rationale: The graph is a natural two-block example in domination theory. The exact enumerator explains how a cut edge changes joint parity across the blocks and separates the bridge pair from all other minimum ordinary cross-clique pairs, giving all coefficients at heterogeneous clique sizes rather than only an extremal number. The reusable even/odd split is the substance beyond the previously covered smallest example.
residual_risks: No bridge formula for arbitrary blocks or for two cliques joined by a longer path is claimed.
